c.tagline: Sicily's baroque port city of black lava stone, at the foot of smoking Mount Etna.

taxi.fareNote: Uber has only a very limited presence; licensed white metered taxis (radio-taxi) are the standard — confirm the meter is running.

emergency.note: 112 is the single European emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing/bag-snatching in the centre and around the station; caution at night

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed baroque heart around Piazza del Duomo, Via Etnea and the theatrical Pescheria fish market, all built from black Etna basalt; best for first-timers who want landmarks, shopping and street life on the doorstep.
The bohemian university quarter of street art, cheap trattorias and a young, arty crowd; lively, affordable and a short walk from the monuments.
A gritty, fast-gentrifying district behind Via Etnea that has become Catania's after-dark hub of bars, live music and clubs; buzzy at night, edgier by day.
The seaside strip southeast of the center along Catania's long sandy beach (La Playa) and its lidos; relaxed and summery, popular with sun-seekers and families.

Catania's elegant shopping avenue and the surrounding residential grid around Via Umberto, lined with boutiques and mid-range hotels; a calmer, well-heeled base a short walk or metro ride from the baroque center.

water.note: Tap water, sourced from Etna's aquifer, is safe to drink.

transit.hours: The metro runs roughly 7:00 AM to 8:45 PM; city buses run from about 5:00 AM to around 10:00 PM, with limited night service.
transit.note: Catania's single metro line (run by Ferrovia Circumetnea) links Nesima and Monte Po with the center at Stesicoro, complemented by AMTS city buses and BRT lines; the compact baroque core is easily walked.
transit.pay: Buy tickets (single ~€1) at tabacchi, machines or the AMTS app and validate on board or at metro gates; day passes are available and metro and bus tickets are integrated.

bus: Catania bus terminal (intercity Interbus, AST, FlixBus coaches across Sicily)
ferry: Port of Catania (seasonal/limited ferry and cruise services)
train: Catania Centrale (Trenitalia to Messina, Syracuse and Palermo)
Ferrovia Circumetnea (narrow-gauge line around Mount Etna)

transit.m: Alibus (AMTS) airport shuttle to Catania Centrale and city center (~20-25 min, frequent)

tip.r: A coperto (cover charge) is common; tipping is not expected — round up or leave a euro or two for good service.

food.name: Pasta alla Norma
food.desc: Catania's emblem dish: tomato sauce, fried aubergine, torn basil and a snowfall of salty ricotta salata, named after Bellini's opera.

places.name: Trattoria di De Fiore
places.note: Legendary slow-cooked home kitchen; the Norma and pasta are made to order, so expect a long, worthwhile wait.

places.name: Me Cumpari Turiddu
places.note: Vintage-styled Sicilian bistro doing a refined Norma with heritage produce; strong local wine list.

places.name: Osteria Antica Marina
places.note: Market-side institution where the Norma sits alongside whatever the boats landed that morning.

food.name: Arancino al ragu
food.desc: In Catania it is masculine and cone-shaped, echoing Etna: fried saffron rice around meat ragu, peas and melting cheese. Also try alla Norma versions.

places.name: Savia
places.note: Open since 1897; marble-counter classic widely rated the best-value arancini and cannoli in the city.

places.name: Pasticceria Spinella
places.note: Long-running pasticceria whose fried rastelleria counter turns over constantly, so everything is hot.

places.name: Etoile d'Or
places.note: Neighbourhood bar-pasticceria popular with locals for morning arancini and rustic savoury pastries.

food.name: Granita con brioche
food.desc: Breakfast, not dessert: almond, mulberry, lemon, coffee or pistachio granita eaten by dunking a soft brioche col tuppo topknot.

places.name: Savia
places.note: Almond granita here is a benchmark; pair it with the housemade brioche col tuppo.

places.name: Prestipino Caffe
places.note: Busy central cafe with a wide granita range and terrace views over Piazza Duomo.

places.name: Pasticceria Spinella
places.note: Reliable all-day granita counter; the pistachio and mulberry flavours are the ones to order.

food.name: Carne di cavallo (horse meat grills)
food.desc: A Catanese obsession: horse steaks, sausages and polpette grilled over charcoal, eaten late at smoky roadside grills.

places.name: La Terrazza del Barone
places.note: Grilled horse meat plus a wide mixed grill, gnocchi and Sicilian desserts in a relaxed dining room.

places.name: Via Plebiscito grill strip
places.note: The classic experience: a run of open-air charcoal grills serving horse steaks and meatballs after dark.

places.name: Osteria Antica Marina
places.note: Good fallback if you want one horse-meat plate alongside the market seafood menu.

food.name: Sarde a beccafico and Pescheria seafood
food.desc: Sardines rolled with breadcrumbs, pine nuts, raisins and orange, plus raw prawns, swordfish and sea urchins straight off the market slabs.

places.name: Scirocco Sicilian Fish Lab
places.note: Fried and grilled market fish served in cones; fast, cheap and always packed at lunch.

places.name: Trattoria La Paglia
places.area: Via Pardo, beside the fish market
places.note: Old-school family trattoria doing sarde, pasta with sardines and market catch at fair prices.

places.name: Osteria Antica Marina
places.note: The upscale market choice; tables spill into the stalls and the raw seafood is excellent.

food.name: Cannoli and cassata siciliana
food.desc: Crisp shells piped to order with sheep's-milk ricotta, and the marzipan-wrapped cassata that anchors Sicilian feast days.

places.name: Savia
places.note: Cannoli filled at the counter so the shell stays shattering-crisp; a city ritual since 1897.

places.name: I Dolci di Nonna Vincenza
places.note: Beautiful old-Sicily pastry room known for cassata, marzipan fruit and ricotta desserts.

places.name: Pasticceria Spinella
places.note: Broad classic range; good for comparing cannoli sizes and ricotta styles in one stop.

food.name: Seltz limone e sale
food.desc: Catania's street refresher: soda water squirted over fresh lemon juice with a pinch of salt, mixed at pavement kiosks year round.

places.name: Chiosco Costa
places.note: One of the best-known historic kiosks; classic salted lemon seltz plus tamarind and mandarin syrups.

places.name: Chiosco Vezzosi
places.note: Long-standing kiosk where locals stop for a seltz on the walk home; syrups made in house.

places.name: Via Etnea kiosks
places.area: Via Etnea and Villa Bellini gates
places.note: Several kiosks along the main street pour seltz all evening; cheapest drink in town.

food.name: Etna wine (Nerello Mascalese and Carricante)
food.desc: Volcanic-soil reds and mineral whites grown on Etna's slopes just above the city, poured by the glass across Catania's wine bars.

places.name: Me Cumpari Turiddu
places.note: Deep Etna list with knowledgeable staff; good small plates to drink alongside.

places.name: Vermut
places.note: Compact natural-leaning wine bar popular with locals for Etna bottles and vermouth.

places.name: Razmataz
places.note: Lively evening wine bar in the student quarter with rotating Sicilian pours by the glass.

landmarks: Piazza del Duomo and the Fontana dell'Elefante
Catania's baroque heart centers on 'u Liotru', a lava-stone elephant carrying an Egyptian obelisk, the city's cherished symbol since 1736.
Mount Etna
Europe's tallest and most active volcano smolders above the city, its lunar craters and lava fields explorable by cable car, jeep, and guided summit hikes.
Cattedrale di Sant'Agata
The city's cathedral, rebuilt in Sicilian baroque after the 1693 earthquake, enshrines beloved patron Saint Agatha and the tomb of composer Vincenzo Bellini.
La Pescheria (Fish Market)
Behind the Duomo, this operatic morning fish market roars with swordfish hawkers and glistening stalls, delivering Sicily's most thrilling sensory spectacle.
Via Etnea
Catania's elegant three-kilometer spine of lava-paved shopping runs arrow-straight toward Etna's snowcapped cone, framed by baroque palazzi and gelato-fueled passeggiata crowds.
Monastero dei Benedettini di San Nicolò l'Arena
One of Europe's largest Benedictine monasteries, a UNESCO baroque labyrinth built over Roman houses and lava flows, now the university's atmospheric humanities campus.
Castello Ursino
Frederick II's brooding 13th-century castle, once seafront until lava flows stranded it inland, now houses the civic museum's art and archaeology collections.
Teatro Romano and Odeon
A 2nd-century Roman theatre of lava stone and marble sits sunken amid ordinary apartment blocks, an evocative collision of ancient and everyday Catania.
Teatro Massimo Bellini
The sumptuous 1890 opera house honoring Catania-born Bellini dazzles with a gilded four-tier horseshoe auditorium celebrated for near-perfect acoustics.
Villa Bellini
The city's loveliest public garden climbs flowered terraces to bandstand belvederes with palm-framed views of Etna floating above the rooftops.

train.note: No international trains. Catania Centrale sits on the Sicilian east-coast line with services north to Taormina and Messina and south to Syracuse; the Intercity and long-distance trains to Rome and Naples are still carried across the Strait of Messina on a train ferry, which makes the journey to Rome around 10 hours. The narrow-gauge Ferrovia Circumetnea loops around Mount Etna as a scenic ride. Booking opens around 120 days ahead.

bus.note: Coaches leave from the terminal beside Catania Centrale. Interbus, SAIS and AST run the Sicilian network to Palermo (about 2h40), Taormina, Syracuse and Agrigento, and are generally faster than the trains. FlixBus covers the long mainland routes via the Messina ferry.

ferry.note: The Malta catamaran runs mainly in the summer months and takes about three hours from Catania's port a short walk from the centre - it is a genuine international crossing, so bring your passport. Grimaldi's overnight ships to Naples and Salerno carry cars and are a comfortable alternative to the long train. Sailings thin out considerably between November and March.

half.name: Syracuse
half.blurb: Ancient Greek city with a monumental Greek theater, Christian catacombs and the baroque island quarter of Ortigia.

half.name: Noto
half.blurb: Baroque UNESCO town rebuilt in golden stone after a 1693 earthquake, known for its ornate facades.
